opus-5.5.text:
I think what excites me most is that code is a domain where we can actually check the output. One of the big problems with large language models in general is that they produce fluent text that may or may not be correct, and we don't have a good way of verifying it. But when the model generates code, or a proof, or some other structured object, we can run it, test it, type-check it, or hand it to a verifier. That gives us a feedback loop that's mostly missing when these systems just produce prose.

So you get a nice division of labor. The language model is very good at the creative, generative part: proposing candidate solutions and drawing on all the patterns it has absorbed from enormous amounts of code. Then a more traditional, formal system checks whether the candidate is right. If it isn't, you can feed the error messages or failed test cases back in and iterate. That combination of a powerful but unreliable generator with a reliable checker is, I think, a very promising architecture for building systems we can actually trust.

The other thing I find exciting is that it lowers the barrier for people to express what they want. Much of programming is translating an intent into a precise formal specification, and LLMs can help bridge that gap, letting domain experts such as scientists, ecologists, and engineers build tools they couldn't build before. Of course, that raises its own questions. How do we know the specification captures what the person meant? How do we test adequately? Those are interesting research problems in their own right. But overall, structured outputs give us a foothold for reliability that I think is really important as we try to move these models from impressive demos to dependable engineering tools.

r002.rationale: It mentions proofs as another verifiable output, but does not describe generating a proof of correctness alongside code to validate that code.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention attackers exploiting hallucinated library dependencies or creating malicious libraries under invented names.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what excites me most is that code is a place where we can actually check the answer. When an LLM writes natural language, we're stuck with the problem of hallucination. The model produces fluent, plausible text, and we have no automatic way to tell whether it's true. But when it produces a program, or a formal proof, or a planning domain, or a SQL query, we can run it. We can compile it, we can test it, we can type-check it, we can hand it to a verifier. So the generation step can be unreliable, and that's fine, because we wrap it in a verification loop that catches the errors.

That's really the paradigm shift for me. Instead of treating the LLM as an oracle that has to be right, we treat it as a proposal mechanism, a very good heuristic search operator, inside a larger system that has a notion of correctness. That's a very old idea in AI, generate and test, but for decades the bottleneck was always the generator. We could write good testers, but we couldn't propose candidates that were anywhere near the right answer. Now we have a generator that's absorbed essentially all of the code humanity has written, and it proposes things that are often almost right. Combine that with a strong checker and you get something that's much more trustworthy than either piece alone.

The other thing I find exciting is that structured objects let us connect LLMs to the rest of computer science and to the rest of AI. If the model can write a PDDL domain, then a classical planner can do the reasoning, and planners are provably correct in ways that chain-of-thought is not. If it can write a probabilistic program, we can do real inference. If it can write a constraint satisfaction model, we hand it to a solver. So rather than asking the language model to do everything in its head, we ask it to translate the messy human problem into a formal representation, and then we use the tools we've spent fifty years building to actually solve it. I think that division of labor is where a lot of the reliable, high-value applications are going to come from.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that, with code and other structured objects, we have ways of checking what the language model produces. If it generates a piece of code, we can compile it, run it, and test it. In some cases, we can use formal methods to verify properties of it. So we don’t have to rely entirely on the model getting the answer right on the first try.

That gives us a very interesting architecture: the language model proposes a solution, another system checks it, and the feedback goes back to the model to help it revise that solution. The model is doing the creative part—suggesting something that might work—and the checker provides a more rigorous constraint.

Of course, passing a set of tests doesn’t establish that a program is correct. The quality of the specification and the checks still matters enormously. But being able to connect generation to an external check makes this a particularly promising direction.

r002.rationale: It mentions using formal methods to verify properties, but does not describe generating a proof of correctness alongside the code.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss attackers creating a malicious library under an LLM-invented dependency name.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that, with code, we have ways of checking what the model produces. If you ask a language model a general question, it can give you a very plausible answer, and determining whether that answer is correct may take a lot of work. With a program, we can at least compile it, run tests, and, in some cases, verify properties of it.

So there's an interesting opportunity to put the language model inside a larger system. The model proposes a solution, we check it, and then we can feed back the errors and ask it to try again. The model doesn't have to get everything right on the first attempt to be useful.

That applies to other structured objects, too, whenever we have constraints or a way to evaluate the result. Passing the checks doesn't necessarily mean we've captured everything we care about—the specification itself can be incomplete. But having that feedback loop gives us a much stronger foundation for building reliable systems.
